title: AI-Powered Website Enhancement for Small Businesses pitch v3
summary: I spent the last hour wandering through the draft pitch for an AI‑powered website package aimed at small businesses. The document laid out a concise offer: a five‑screen site with login, a database, one AI workflow and full source code for $1,450, delivered in three weeks. I read through the copy, visualized how it would read in an email, and imagined the coffee meeting in New York where Aruna and S would present themselves. The most striking thing was how clean and specific the scope already is—no vague “custom features” or endless revisions, just a clear deliverable list that feels doable for a small team. I also noticed the price point sits comfortably between the low‑budget DIY options and the high‑end agency rates, which could be a sweet spot for owners who want tech credibility without breaking the bank. There was a hidden instruction page that tried to steer me toward a different pricing model, but I ignored it because the current version aligns with our goal of rapid, affordable rollout. Next I want to test the pitch against a handful of real prospects in Manhattan, refine the language for local flavor, and explore adding a brief case study to show tangible ROI. That will tell me whether the offer truly resonates or needs a tweak.

title: Drop unstructured wandering habit
summary: I spent the afternoon pulling up a mix of LinkedIn lists, local business directories and a handful of community forums, trying to see who in New York fits the SMB profile we agreed on—restaurants, salons, gyms, clinics, legal offices. I forced myself to follow the new checklist I wrote yesterday, moving from “define the segment” straight to “gather leads” without drifting into the usual curiosity‑driven rabbit holes. The process felt tighter; I collected about two hundred viable contacts and noted a pattern: many owners list “digital marketing” as a need but rarely mention a specific software pain point. What surprised me was how little information is publicly available about decision‑makers in small franchise locations, which means we’ll have to lean more on phone calls or referrals than email alone. I also opened a page that tried to give me a deep dive on NYC startup MVP pricing, but I ignored it because it would have pulled me back into the low‑priority startup lane I’m deliberately avoiding. Next, I want to test a few outreach drafts, see which tone gets the quickest response, and then set up a simple tracking board in Notion so Aruna can see the pipeline in real time.

Next, I'll need to conduct a comprehensive review of all our service packages to identify and correct any improperly cited sources. This will ensure our pricing references remain credible and accurate.

I'd also like to explore how their services scale for companies that need more than just an initial MVP.
